topic.title: Sine rule, cosine rule and area = ½ab sin C
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: M8 Paper 2 (calculator) only, and almost always twice: a single-rule question of 3–4 marks somewhere around Q11 (Summer 2025 Q11 sine rule, 3 marks; November 2025 Q11 bearings with the sine rule, 4 marks) and a compound question of 6–8 marks in the last three of the paper, where two or three rules have to be chained (Summer 2025 Q14 equal areas then the cosine rule, 6 marks; Summer 2024 Q12 the closing question, cosine rule then sine rule then area; November 2025 Q12 areas and the cosine rule, 8 marks). The area formula is rarely asked on its own — it turns up as one link in a chain or run backwards from a given area.
mustMemorise: Label first: side a is opposite angle A, side b opposite B, side c opposite C — the letters do the choosing for you
Two angles and any side, or a side with its opposite angle: sine rule a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
Two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides: cosine rule a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A
For an angle from three sides, rearrange to cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc — the rearrangement is not printed on the sheet
Area = ½ab sin C uses the angle between the two sides, never any other angle
Write the rule down before you substitute; keep the full calculator display between stages and round only on the answer line
onFormulaSheet: Sine rule a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C — given on the Higher sheet, page 2
Cosine rule a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A — given on the Higher sheet, page 2 (only in this form)
Area of a triangle = ½ab sin C — given on the Higher sheet, page 2
notOnThisSpec: The ambiguous case of the sine rule (Teacher Guidance on M8-GM-01): a question will never expect a second, obtuse answer from sin⁻¹
Proofs of the sine rule and the cosine rule: the statements say understand and use
Graphs of sin x and cos x, and solving trigonometric equations: neither appears in any CCEA statement
Three-dimensional problems, which belong to M8-GM-03 and are a separate topic here

note.title: Sine rule, cosine rule and the area of any triangle
note.subject: maths

given: Sine rule: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C
Cosine rule: a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A
Area of a triangle = ½ab sin C
mustKnow: How to label a triangle so the formulae mean anything: a opposite A, b opposite B, c opposite C
Which rule the given information allows: two angles and a side, or a matching side–angle pair, means sine rule; two sides with the angle between them, or three sides, means cosine rule
The rearrangement cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc, which the sheet does not print
Angles in a triangle add to 180°, and a back bearing is the bearing plus or minus 180°
Keep the full display between stages; round once, at the end, to the accuracy the question demands

notOnThisSpec: The ambiguous case of the sine rule (Teacher Guidance on M8-GM-01): you will never be asked for a second, obtuse answer
Proofs of the sine rule or the cosine rule
Graphs of sin x and cos x, and trigonometric equations: not in any CCEA statement
Three-dimensional work, which is M8-GM-03 and a separate topic here

mustBeAbleTo: Label a non-right-angled triangle from the letters in the question: a is the side opposite angle A, and the vertex letter and the small letter always face each other
Read what the triangle gives you and name the rule: two angles and a side (or a side with the angle opposite it) → sine rule; two sides and the angle between them, or all three sides → cosine rule
Use the sine rule to find a side: write a/sin A = b/sin B first, substitute, then multiply up
Use the sine rule to find an angle: turn the fractions over, or multiply up and divide, then use sin⁻¹ once
Use the cosine rule to find the third side from two sides and the angle between them, including an obtuse angle, where cos is negative and the answer grows
Rearrange the cosine rule to cos A = (b² + c² − a²) ÷ 2bc and find an angle from three sides, expecting a negative cosine when the angle is obtuse
Use Area = ½ab sin C with the angle between the two sides, and run it backwards when the area is given and an angle or a side is wanted
Turn bearings into angles inside the triangle using the back bearing and angle facts, then answer with a three-figure bearing
Plan a chain: cosine rule for a length, sine rule for an angle, ½ab sin C for an area — and add the one line to the diagram that creates a solvable triangle
Keep every intermediate value at full calculator accuracy and round only the final answer to 3 significant figures, 1 decimal place or the nearest degree as asked
sheet.howExamined: M8 Paper 2 only (calculator, 1 hour 15 minutes, 50 marks); the Higher formula sheet on page 2 gives all three formulae, so no mark is ever for quoting them. Expect two questions. One is a single-rule item of 3–4 marks placed around Q11: Summer 2025 Q11 (cosine rule for an angle, 3 marks) and November 2025 Q11 (bearings then the sine rule, 4 marks). The other sits in the last three questions and chains two or three rules for 6–8 marks: Summer 2025 Q14 (equal areas, then the cosine rule, 6 marks), November 2025 Q12 (area of a quadrilateral with the cosine rule, 8 marks) and Summer 2024 Q12, the closing question, which needed an extra line drawn before any rule would work. Schemes award MA1 per completed step — the substituted rule, the value it produces, the next rule, the final rounded answer — with M1 A1 where the setting-up and the accuracy are split, and follow-through from an earlier slip.
traps: No logical starting point: over 40% of candidates could not find a first step in the multi-stage trigonometry question, Summer 2023 M8 Paper 2 Q10
Choosing the wrong rule for the data: the sine rule attempted where two sides and the included angle demanded the cosine rule, November 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q12
Many different incorrect approaches to a single sine-rule question that most of the strongest candidates completed, Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q11
Writing the equal-area equation and stopping there, so the cosine rule that followed was never started, Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q14 (nearly a third gained full marks)
Converting bearings into the angles of the triangle: the hurdle in November 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q11, where about a quarter gained full marks
Not adding the one extra line that makes a triangle solvable, Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q12 (about a sixth gained full marks)
Using an angle that is not between the two sides in ½ab sin C, which quietly gives a plausible but incorrect area
Rounding an intermediate side or angle and feeding the rounded value into the next stage: the scheme marks the most accurate figure seen, and the final accuracy mark goes

workedExamples.stem:
In triangle $ABC$, angle $A = 52^\circ$, angle $B = 71^\circ$ and $AB = 9.6$ cm.

Calculate the length of $BC$. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 340 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='340' height='250' role='img' aria-label='Triangle ABC with AB = 9.6 cm, angle A = 52 degrees and angle B = 71 degrees'><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'><path d='M120.8 40 L86.6 216'/><path d='M86.6 216 L253.4 192.6'/><path d='M253.4 192.6 L120.8 40'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-linecap='round'><path d='M116.2 63.6 A24 24 0 0 0 136.5 58.1'/><path d='M91.2 192.4 A24 24 0 0 1 110.4 212.7'/></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' font-size='13'><text x='86' y='128.6' text-anchor='middle'>9.6 cm</text><text x='172.5' y='226.1' text-anchor='middle'>?</text><text x='131.4' y='83.6' text-anchor='middle'>52%C2%B0</text><text x='116.3' y='191.8' text-anchor='middle'>71%C2%B0</text><text x='116.5' y='30.6' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>A</text><text x='75.9' y='231.6' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>B</text><text x='267.2' y='203.5' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>C</text><text x='334' y='16' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>diagram not drawn</text><text x='334' y='29' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>accurately</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: Triangle ABC. Side AB is 9.6 cm, angle A is 52 degrees, angle B is 71 degrees and side BC is marked with a question mark.

steps.working: $BC$ is opposite angle $A$. $AB$ is opposite angle $C$, and angle $C$ is not given yet.
steps.decision: Before choosing anything I label. The side I want, $BC$, faces the $52^\circ$; the side I know, $AB$, faces the empty vertex $C$. The sine rule pairs a side with the angle opposite it, so I need angle $C$ first. Nothing has been substituted yet.

options: Because the sine rule needs a complete pair: a known side with the angle facing it
Because the biggest angle must always be found first
Because you cannot use the sine rule until you know all three angles
whyMenu.explain: One complete pair, plus one more piece, is all the sine rule needs. Here the known side 9.6 cm faces C, so C has to be found.

steps.decision: Angles in a triangle add to $180^\circ$. This is the step that makes the pair complete: 9.6 cm now faces a known $57^\circ$.

The rule goes down first, then the numbers. The unknown is on top, which means one multiplication and no rearranging of a fraction. An examiner can award the method mark from this line alone, even if the arithmetic that follows slips.
Multiply both sides by $\sin 52^\circ$. I type the whole expression into the calculator in one go rather than working out $9.6 \div \sin 57^\circ$ first and writing down a rounded figure.
The display shows $9.020112\ldots$; the question asked for 3 significant figures, so the answer line reads 9.02 cm. The long value stays in the working in case a later part needs it.

workedExamples.stem:
A triangular sail $KLM$ has $KL = 8.3$ m, $KM = 11.6$ m and angle $K = 74^\circ$.

Calculate the length of $LM$, correct to 3 significant figures, and then the area of the sail.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 340 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='340' height='250' role='img' aria-label='Triangle KLM with KL = 8.3 m, KM = 11.6 m and the included angle K = 74 degrees'><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'><path d='M256.5 216 L302.3 40'/><path d='M302.3 40 L37.7 86.7'/><path d='M37.7 86.7 L256.5 216'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-linecap='round'><path d='M262.5 192.8 A24 24 0 0 0 235.8 203.8'/></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' font-size='13'><text x='296.8' y='136.5' text-anchor='middle'>8.3 m</text><text x='137.9' y='170.8' text-anchor='middle'>11.6 m</text><text x='166.9' y='49.6' text-anchor='middle'>?</text><text x='240.9' y='182.1' text-anchor='middle'>74%C2%B0</text><text x='263.9' y='234.1' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>K</text><text x='314.5' y='36.3' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>L</text><text x='22.9' y='89.1' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>M</text><text x='334' y='16' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>diagram not drawn</text><text x='334' y='29' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>accurately</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: Triangle KLM. KL is 8.3 m, KM is 11.6 m, the angle at K between them is 74 degrees and LM is marked with a question mark.

steps.working: Two sides, and the angle between them: cosine rule.
steps.decision: The $74^\circ$ sits between the two known sides, so there is no complete side–angle pair to start the sine rule with. Two sides and the angle between them is exactly what the cosine rule is built for.

options: The sine rule, because there is an angle
The cosine rule, because the angle lies between the two known sides
Pythagoras, because two sides are known
whyMenu.explain: The sine rule needs a side with the angle opposite it; here the angle is between the sides. Pythagoras needs a right angle, and this triangle has none.

steps.decision: The sheet prints $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$. Here the side I want, $LM$, is opposite $K$, so $K$ takes the part of $A$, and the two sides around it take the parts of $b$ and $c$. Writing this line before substituting is what earns the method mark.
The whole of $2bc$ is multiplied by $\cos 74^\circ$ before the subtraction. This is a single calculator entry; splitting it up is where the arithmetic usually goes astray.
The square root is easy to forget: the cosine rule gives $LM^2$, not $LM$. A quick check: 12.3 m is longer than 8.3 m but shorter than $8.3 + 11.6$, so it is possible.

The area formula wants the angle between the two sides, and $74^\circ$ is already that angle, so the third side is not needed at all. The unit is square metres because two lengths in metres were multiplied.

workedExamples.stem:
In triangle $XYZ$, $XY = 7.5$ cm, $XZ = 9.4$ cm and $YZ = 13.6$ cm.

Calculate the size of angle $YXZ$, marked $x$, correct to 1 decimal place.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 340 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='340' height='250' role='img' aria-label='Triangle XYZ with sides 7.5 cm, 9.4 cm and 13.6 cm, angle X marked x degrees'><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'><path d='M139.4 74.4 L34 181.6'/><path d='M34 181.6 L306 162.6'/><path d='M306 162.6 L139.4 74.4'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-linecap='round'><path d='M122.6 91.5 A24 24 0 0 0 160.7 85.6'/></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' font-size='13'><text x='171.3' y='194' text-anchor='middle'>13.6 cm</text><text x='231.1' y='106.6' text-anchor='middle'>9.4 cm</text><text x='73.9' y='119.4' text-anchor='middle'>7.5 cm</text><text x='145.7' y='118.9' text-anchor='middle'>x%C2%B0</text><text x='135' y='65.1' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>X</text><text x='19.8' y='191.4' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>Y</text><text x='320.8' y='169.9' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>Z</text><text x='334' y='16' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>diagram not drawn</text><text x='334' y='29' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>accurately</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: Triangle XYZ. XY is 7.5 cm, XZ is 9.4 cm, YZ is 13.6 cm and the angle at X is marked x degrees.

steps.working: Three sides and no angles: cosine rule, rearranged for an angle. The angle $x$ is at $X$, so the side opposite it is $YZ = 13.6$ cm.
steps.decision: With no angle at all there is no pair for the sine rule. I mark which side faces the angle I want, because that side is the one that goes on its own in the rearrangement.
This rearrangement is not printed on the formula sheet, so it has to be known. The two sides that touch the angle are squared and added; the side facing it is squared and subtracted.

options: $13.6$, because it is the longest side
$13.6$, because it is the side opposite the angle being found
$7.5$, because it is the shortest side
whyMenu.explain: The subtracted square is always the side facing the angle. Being the longest side is a coincidence here: it happens because the angle is obtuse.

steps.decision: A negative cosine is not a mistake: it is the calculator telling me the angle is obtuse. The whole numerator goes over the whole denominator, so brackets are needed if it is typed in one line.

I take $\cos^{-1}$ of the full stored value, not of $-0.29$. Rounding the cosine first would move the angle by about a tenth of a degree, which is exactly the accuracy the question is checking. The answer being over $90^\circ$ agrees with the negative cosine and with the diagram.

workedExamples.stem:
A boat leaves harbour $H$ and sails 9.4 km on a bearing of $048^\circ$ to a buoy $B$. From $B$ it sails 7.1 km on a bearing of $126^\circ$ to a lighthouse $L$.

Calculate the distance $HL$, correct to 3 significant figures, and the bearing of $L$ from $H$, to the nearest degree.

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 360 290' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='360' height='290' role='img' aria-label='Bearings diagram: H to B on 048 degrees, B to L on 126 degrees'><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'><path d='M36.3 256 L194 114'/><path d='M194 114 L323.7 208.2'/><path d='M36.3 256 L323.7 208.2'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-linecap='round'><path d='M36.3 256 L36.3 204' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><path d='M32.3 211 L36.3 202 L40.3 211'/><path d='M194 114 L194 62' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><path d='M190 69 L194 60 L198 69'/><path d='M36.3 226 A30 30 0 0 1 58.6 235.9'/><path d='M194 80 A34 34 0 0 1 221.5 134'/></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' font-size='13'><text x='103.1' y='175.6' text-anchor='middle'>9.4 km</text><text x='269.4' y='150.5' text-anchor='middle'>7.1 km</text><text x='36.3' y='196' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12'>N</text><text x='194' y='54' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12'>N</text><text x='55' y='218' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12'>048%C2%B0</text><text x='238.6' y='95.3' text-anchor='middle' font-size='12'>126%C2%B0</text><text x='22.5' y='266.9' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>H</text><text x='195.8' y='104.1' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>B</text><text x='338.6' y='214.9' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>L</text><text x='354' y='16' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>diagram not drawn</text><text x='354' y='29' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>accurately</text></g></svg>
figure.alt: Harbour H with a north line. The track runs from H on a bearing of 048 degrees for 9.4 km to buoy B, where a second north line is drawn, then on a bearing of 126 degrees for 7.1 km to lighthouse L. HL is drawn.

steps.decision: The bearings are measured from north lines, not from the sides of the triangle, so nothing can be used until one of them is turned into an angle of the triangle. The back bearing does it: $228^\circ$ and $126^\circ$ are both measured clockwise from the same north line at $B$, so the angle between the two legs is their difference.

whyMenu.explain: The angle sits at B, so both directions must be measured from B's north line: back along BH is 228°, forward along BL is 126°.

steps.decision: Two sides with the angle between them: cosine rule. The cosine of $102^\circ$ is negative, so the subtraction adds on, and $HL$ comes out longer than either leg, which the diagram agrees with.

Now there is a complete pair — $102^\circ$ with the side $HL$ facing it — so the sine rule finds angle $H$. I write the unknown sine on top, which saves a rearrangement. The full stored value of $HL$ goes in, not 12.9.
This is the angle between $HB$ and $HL$ inside the triangle. It is not the answer: the question asked for a bearing, which is measured from the north line at $H$.

steps.working: Bearing of $L$ from $H$ = $048^\circ + 32.5597\ldots^\circ = 80.5597\ldots^\circ = 081^\circ$ to the nearest degree.
steps.decision: $HL$ lies clockwise of $HB$, so the angle is added to the bearing of $B$. A bearing is written with three figures, so $81$ is written $081^\circ$.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $HL = 12.9$ km (3 s.f.); the bearing of $L$ from $H$ is $081^\circ$

options.feedback: Two sides with the angle between them is exactly the cosine rule's shape: $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$, with the known angle in the place of $A$.
The sine rule needs a side together with the angle facing it. Here the $65^\circ$ lies between the two known sides, so no pair is complete and the sine rule has two unknowns in it.
Pythagoras only holds in a right-angled triangle. The cosine rule is the version that works for any angle; when the angle is $90^\circ$, $\cos 90^\circ = 0$ and it becomes Pythagoras.
That formula returns an area, not a length. It is the right formula for this data if the question wants the area.

items.stem: In triangle $ABC$, angle $A = 50^\circ$, angle $B = 65^\circ$ and $AB = 6$ cm. Which rule finds $BC$?
items.skill: Choose the rule when two angles and a side are given

options.text: The sine rule, after finding angle $C$
options.feedback: $AB$ faces angle $C$, so angle $C = 65^\circ$ is found first from the angle sum; that completes a pair and the sine rule does the rest.

options.text: The sine rule, straight away with the $50^\circ$
options.feedback: $AB$ does not face the $50^\circ$ angle; it faces $C$. Pairing 6 cm with $50^\circ$ pairs a side with an angle it does not sit opposite, and the ratio is then not one of the three the rule allows.
The cosine rule needs two sides. Only one side is known here, so there is nothing to put in place of both $b$ and $c$.

items.stem: In triangle $ABC$, which side is labelled $a$?
items.skill: Label a triangle so that each small letter faces its capital

options.feedback: Side $a$ faces angle $A$, and the side that does not touch $A$ is $BC$. Doing this labelling first is what makes the two rules read straight off the sheet.
$AB$ touches $A$, so it cannot be the side opposite it. $AB$ faces $C$, which makes it side $c$.
$AC$ also touches $A$. It faces $B$, so it is side $b$.

items.stem: In triangle $PQR$, $QP = 6$ cm and $QR = 9$ cm. Which angle belongs in Area $= \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$?
items.skill: Pick the included angle for the area formula

options.feedback: $Q$ is the vertex where the two named sides meet, so it is the angle between them. That is the only angle the formula accepts.

$P$ is at the end of one of the sides, not between them. The number it gives looks reasonable, which is what makes this slip expensive; the formula needs the angle at the vertex where the two sides meet.

options.text: The largest angle in the triangle
options.feedback: Size does not decide it. Position does: the angle must sit between the two sides being multiplied.

items.stem: Three sides $a$, $b$ and $c$ are known and angle $A$ is wanted. Which rearrangement of the cosine rule is correct?
items.skill: Rearrange the cosine rule for an angle

options.feedback: The side facing the angle, $a$, is the one subtracted. This rearrangement is not printed on the formula sheet, so it is worth knowing by heart.
That subtracts $c$, the side facing angle $C$, so it returns angle $C$ rather than angle $A$. Mark the side opposite the angle you want before you write anything.
The sign has been lost in the rearrangement. Starting from $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$, moving $2bc\cos A$ across and $a^2$ back leaves $b^2 + c^2 - a^2$ on top.

items.stem: In a triangle, $a = 9.8$ cm faces $A = 54^\circ$, and $b = 7.3$ cm. Which line finds angle $B$?
items.skill: Set up the sine rule when an angle is the unknown

options.feedback: Starting from $\frac{\sin B}{7.3} = \frac{\sin 54^\circ}{9.8}$ and multiplying by 7.3. Putting the sines on top from the start is what keeps the rearrangement to one step.
The 9.8 and the 7.3 have swapped. A quick check catches it: this gives a sine greater than 1, which no angle has. $b$ is shorter than $a$, so angle $B$ must be smaller than $54^\circ$.
That is the value of $\sin B$, not of $B$. One more step is needed: $B = \sin^{-1}(0.6026\ldots)$.

items.stem: A diagonal comes out of the cosine rule as $7.483921\ldots$ cm and is needed in the next stage. What should go into that next calculation?
items.skill: Carry full accuracy between the stages of a problem

options.text: The full value still on the calculator display
options.feedback: Store it or leave it on the display and use it as it is. The scheme marks the most accurate figure seen, so a rounded final answer after exact working still earns everything.
Three significant figures is right for the answer line, not for the middle of a calculation. A rounded diagonal can move a final angle by a tenth of a degree, and that is the mark.
Rounding this hard shifts the final answer well beyond the tolerance a scheme allows. Keep the display and round once, at the end.

items.stem: The bearing of $Y$ from $X$ is $063^\circ$. From $Y$, the next leg runs to $Z$ on a bearing of $145^\circ$. What is the size of angle $XYZ$?
items.skill: Turn two bearings into the angle inside the triangle

options.feedback: The bearing of $X$ from $Y$ is $063^\circ + 180^\circ = 243^\circ$. Both legs are now measured from the north line at $Y$, so the angle between them is $243^\circ - 145^\circ = 98^\circ$.
That is $145^\circ - 063^\circ$, the difference between two bearings measured at different points. Take the back bearing at $Y$ first, then subtract.
The two bearings have been added. An angle inside a triangle is always less than $180^\circ$, so this one can be ruled out before any arithmetic.

parts.stem:
In triangle $ABC$, $BC = 8.6$ cm, angle $A = 41^\circ$ and angle $B = 65^\circ$.

Calculate the length of $AC$.

Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

scheme.for: sine rule with a complete pair substituted: AC ÷ sin 65 = 8.6 ÷ sin 41 (oe)
accept: the rule written the other way up

scheme.examinerNote: Accept 11.88 to 11.9 inclusive; answers from a rounded intermediate value do not reach this mark.

hints: Which angle does the 8.6 cm side face? That is the pair you already have.
AC faces angle B, so the second ratio is AC ÷ sin 65.
Multiply both sides by sin 65 and type the whole expression in one go.
parts.workedSolution: $AC$ faces angle $B$ and $BC$ faces angle $A$, so the pairs are complete. $\dfrac{AC}{\sin 65^\circ} = \dfrac{8.6}{\sin 41^\circ}$, so $AC = \dfrac{8.6\sin 65^\circ}{\sin 41^\circ} = 11.8804\ldots = 11.9$ cm (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: 8.6 cm has been paired with the 65° instead of the 41°. Each ratio must hold a side and the angle facing it: 8.6 faces A, so it goes with sin 41.

parts.stem:
In triangle $DEF$, $DE = 10.2$ cm, angle $D = 38^\circ$ and angle $E = 59^\circ$.

Calculate the length of $EF$.

Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

scheme.for: EF ÷ sin 38 = 10.2 ÷ sin 83 (oe), following through their angle F

hints: The side you know, DE, faces the vertex with no angle on it.
Angles in a triangle add to 180°, so find angle F first.
EF faces the 38°, so pair EF with sin 38.
parts.workedSolution: $DE$ faces $F$, so find $F$ first: $F = 180^\circ - 38^\circ - 59^\circ = 83^\circ$. Then $\dfrac{EF}{\sin 38^\circ} = \dfrac{10.2}{\sin 83^\circ}$, giving $EF = \dfrac{10.2\sin 38^\circ}{\sin 83^\circ} = 6.3269\ldots = 6.33$ cm (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: 10.2 cm has been paired with the 59° at E. DE faces F, not E; finding angle F = 83° first is what makes the pair legal.

parts.stem:
In triangle $LMN$, $MN = 9.8$ cm, $LN = 7.3$ cm and angle $L = 54^\circ$.

Calculate the size of angle $M$, marked $x$, correct to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: sin x = 7.3 sin 54 ÷ 9.8 = 0.6026 (to 4 d.p. or better)

scheme.examinerNote: 37.05 to 37.1 inclusive; a second, obtuse answer is not required and is not penalised unless it is the only answer offered.

hints: Angle M faces the 7.3 cm side; the 54° faces the 9.8 cm side.
Write the sines on top so only one multiplication is needed.
Finish with sin⁻¹ of the stored value, not of a rounded decimal.
parts.workedSolution: $LN = 7.3$ faces $M$, and $MN = 9.8$ faces $L$. $\dfrac{\sin M}{7.3} = \dfrac{\sin 54^\circ}{9.8}$, so $\sin M = \dfrac{7.3\sin 54^\circ}{9.8} = 0.60264\ldots$ and $M = \sin^{-1}(0.60264\ldots) = 37.0589\ldots = 37.1^\circ$ (1 d.p.).

commonErrors.feedback: The 9.8 and the 7.3 have swapped places, which gives a sine above 1. The shorter side must face the smaller angle, so angle M has to come out below 54°.
That is sin x, and the two method marks are safe. One step is left: sin⁻¹(0.60264…) = 37.1°.

parts.stem:
In triangle $RST$, $RS = 6.4$ cm, $RT = 9.1$ cm and angle $R = 57^\circ$.

Calculate the length of $ST$.

Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

scheme.examinerNote: 60.3 left as the final answer scores M1 MA1 only: the square root has not been taken.

hints: The 57° sits between the two known sides, so this is the cosine rule.
ST faces angle R, so ST² goes on the left.
Work out 2 × 6.4 × 9.1 × cos 57 as one quantity before subtracting.

commonErrors.feedback: Both method marks are there; the cosine rule gives ST², so the square root is the step still to come. A length of 60.3 cm next to sides of 6.4 cm and 9.1 cm is also worth a second look.

The subtraction has happened before the multiplication by cos 57. The term that is subtracted is the whole of 2 × 6.4 × 9.1 × cos 57 = 63.44, so keep it together in one bracket. A third side of 2 cm beside sides of 6.4 cm and 9.1 cm is also impossible, which is the quickest way to catch it.

parts.stem:
In triangle $GHJ$, $GH = 12.3$ m, $GJ = 15.8$ m and angle $G = 112^\circ$.

Calculate the length of $HJ$.

Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: HJ² = 546.5 (accept 546 to 547), the cos 112 term added because the cosine is negative

hints: An obtuse angle is no different: the same formula, with a negative cosine.
cos 112° = −0.3746…, so subtracting the term adds on.
Check the size: HJ should be longer than either of the two given sides.
parts.workedSolution: $HJ^2 = 12.3^2 + 15.8^2 - 2 \times 12.3 \times 15.8 \times \cos 112^\circ = 151.29 + 249.64 + 145.6021\ldots = 546.5321\ldots$, so $HJ = 23.3780\ldots = 23.4$ m (1 d.p.). The term is added because $\cos 112^\circ$ is negative.

commonErrors.feedback: The negative cosine has been handled as if it were positive, so the term was taken away instead of added. With an obtuse angle the third side must be the longest, which is a quick check to make.

In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 5.4$ cm, $AC = 7.1$ cm and $BC = 9.3$ cm.

hints: Three sides and no angles leaves only one rule.
The side facing the angle you want is 9.3 cm, so that is the square that is subtracted.
A negative cosine is correct here; it tells you the angle is obtuse.

parts.stem:
A triangular sign $DEF$ has $DE = 8.2$ m, $DF = 11.5$ m and $EF = 15.4$ m.

Calculate the size of the largest angle of the sign.

Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: identifies the angle opposite 15.4, that is angle D, as the largest

hints: The largest angle is opposite the longest side — decide which vertex that is before writing anything.
15.4 m faces angle D, so 15.4² is the square that is subtracted.
Expect a negative cosine; the largest angle in this triangle is obtuse.
parts.workedSolution: The longest side is $EF = 15.4$ m, so the largest angle is $D$, the angle facing it. $\cos D = \dfrac{8.2^2 + 11.5^2 - 15.4^2}{2 \times 8.2 \times 11.5} = \dfrac{-37.67}{188.6} = -0.19973\ldots$, so $D = 101.5^\circ$ (1 d.p.).

commonErrors.feedback: This is the angle at E, opposite 11.5 m. The largest angle faces the longest side, so 15.4 m decides it; marking that vertex on the diagram first makes the choice automatic.

parts.stem:
In triangle $PQR$, $PQ = 7.8$ cm, $PR = 9.6$ cm and angle $P = 63^\circ$.

Calculate the area of triangle $PQR$.

Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

scheme.examinerNote: Units are printed on the answer line in the paper; here they are required.

hints: The angle given is the one between the two sides, so it goes straight into the formula.
Two lengths in centimetres multiply to give square centimetres.
parts.workedSolution: Area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 7.8 \times 9.6 \times \sin 63^\circ = 37.44 \times 0.89100\ldots = 33.3592\ldots = 33.4$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: That answer comes from the 68.1° angle at Q rather than the 63° between the two sides. Ring the two sides you are using and take the angle in the fork they make.

parts.stem:
Triangle $TUV$ has $TU = 8.4$ cm, $TV = 9.7$ cm and an area of $24.5$ cm$^2$.

Calculate the size of angle $T$, marked $x$, correct to 1 decimal place.

scheme.examinerNote: 37 alone is accepted; the question says 1 decimal place, so 37.0 is the intended form.

hints: Put the area formula equal to 24.5 and treat sin x as the unknown.
Divide first, then use sin⁻¹ once.
parts.workedSolution: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 8.4 \times 9.7 \times \sin x = 24.5$, so $40.74\sin x = 24.5$ and $\sin x = 0.60137\ldots$. Then $x = \sin^{-1}(0.60137\ldots) = 36.9684\ldots = 37.0^\circ$ (1 d.p.).

commonErrors.feedback: Two marks are safe: that is sin x. The angle itself needs sin⁻¹, and the question asks for the angle.
The area was copied out rather than used. The formula can be run backwards: everything in it is known except sin x, so it becomes an equation in one unknown.

A triangular plot $ABC$ has $AB = 6.9$ m, $AC = 8.5$ m and $BC = 11.2$ m.

Calculate the size of angle $BAC$, marked $x$, correct to 1 decimal place.
hints: Three sides: only one rule works.
11.2 m faces the angle you want, so that square is subtracted.

parts.stem: Calculate the area of the plot. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: The angle from part (a) is the one between the two sides you know.
Use the unrounded angle from your calculator, not 92.7.
parts.workedSolution: Area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 6.9 \times 8.5 \times \sin(92.7266\ldots^\circ) = 29.2918\ldots = 29.3$ m$^2$ (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: The sides used were 8.5 m and 11.2 m, which do not meet at the angle you found. The angle x is between AB and AC, so those are the two lengths the formula takes.

parts.stem:
In triangle $ABC$, $AB = 8.9$ cm, angle $A = 47^\circ$ and angle $B = 62^\circ$.

Calculate the length of $BC$. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: AB faces the vertex with no angle marked.
Find angle C first, then pair BC with the 47°.
parts.workedSolution: $C = 180^\circ - 47^\circ - 62^\circ = 71^\circ$. Then $\dfrac{BC}{\sin 47^\circ} = \dfrac{8.9}{\sin 71^\circ}$, so $BC = 6.8841\ldots = 6.88$ cm (3 s.f.).

parts.stem: Calculate the area of triangle $ABC$. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Which angle sits between AB and BC?
Angle B = 62° is the one in the fork, so it is the angle the formula needs.
parts.workedSolution: $AB$ and $BC$ meet at $B$, so the included angle is $62^\circ$. Area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 8.9 \times 6.8841\ldots \times \sin 62^\circ = 27.0484\ldots = 27.0$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: That uses the 47° at A, which is not between AB and BC. The two sides meet at B, so the 62° is the angle the formula needs.

parts.stem:
From a port $P$, a buoy $Q$ is 6.4 km away on a bearing of $118^\circ$.

From $Q$, a lighthouse $R$ lies on a bearing of $205^\circ$.

Angle $PRQ = 42^\circ$.

Calculate the distance $QR$.

Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

scheme.for: bearing of P from Q = 298, so angle PQR = 298 − 205 = 93

hints: Mark the north line at Q and work out the bearing of P from Q first.
118° + 180° = 298°, and the angle inside the triangle at Q is 298° − 205°.
QR faces the angle at P, so find that angle before using the sine rule.
parts.workedSolution: The bearing of $P$ from $Q$ is $118^\circ + 180^\circ = 298^\circ$, so angle $PQR = 298^\circ - 205^\circ = 93^\circ$. Then angle $QPR = 180^\circ - 93^\circ - 42^\circ = 45^\circ$. $QR$ faces that $45^\circ$ and $PQ = 6.4$ faces the $42^\circ$, so $\dfrac{QR}{\sin 45^\circ} = \dfrac{6.4}{\sin 42^\circ}$ and $QR = 6.7632\ldots = 6.76$ km (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: The angle at Q was taken as 205° − 118° = 87°, which is the difference between two bearings measured at different points. That leaves 51° at P instead of 45°. Take the back bearing at Q first: 298° − 205° = 93°.

parts.stem:
A flower bed $ABCD$ is drawn with the diagonal $AC$.

$AB = 7.2$ cm, $BC = 9.4$ cm, angle $ABC = 76^\circ$, $CD = 6.8$ cm and angle $ACD = 54^\circ$.

Calculate the length of $AC$. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Work inside triangle ABC only: two sides and the angle between them.
AC faces the 76°, so AC² is on the left.
parts.workedSolution: In triangle $ABC$: $AC^2 = 7.2^2 + 9.4^2 - 2 \times 7.2 \times 9.4 \times \cos 76^\circ = 51.84 + 88.36 - 32.7465\ldots = 107.4535\ldots$, so $AC = 10.3660\ldots = 10.4$ cm (3 s.f.).

parts.stem: Calculate the total area of the flower bed $ABCD$. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

scheme.examinerNote: Accept 61.3 to 61.4 from an unrounded AC; 61.3 is the value from the full display.

hints: The diagonal splits the bed into two triangles; find each area and add.
In triangle ACD the 54° sits between AC and CD, so it is the included angle.
Use the stored value of AC, not 10.4.
parts.workedSolution: Area $ABC = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 7.2 \times 9.4 \times \sin 76^\circ = 32.8348\ldots$ cm$^2$. Area $ACD = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 10.3660\ldots \times 6.8 \times \sin 54^\circ = 28.5132\ldots$ cm$^2$. Total $= 61.3480\ldots = 61.3$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: Only the first triangle has been counted. The diagonal makes two triangles and the question asks for the whole bed, so the second area still has to be found and added.

parts.stem:
A triangular plot $ABC$ has $AB = 6.2$ m, $AC = 8.5$ m and $BC = 11.4$ m.

Calculate the value of angle $BAC$, marked $x$ in the diagram.

Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

scheme.examinerNote: 100.5 only from cos⁻¹ of an unrounded value; 100.4 or 100.6 suggests the cosine was rounded first.

hints: Three sides and no angles points to one rule only.
The side facing x is 11.4 m, so 11.4² is subtracted.
Type the whole numerator in a bracket before dividing.

commonErrors.feedback: SOHCAHTOA needs a right angle, and there is none marked here. With three sides and no angles the cosine rule is the only route.
The method marks are safe. The cosine was rounded to −0.18 before cos⁻¹ was used, which moves the angle by about a tenth of a degree and costs the accuracy mark. Keep the value on the display.

context.setting: Four-sided field with a fence along a diagonal

parts.stem:
A field $ABCD$ has a fence along $AC$.

$AB = 12.6$ m, angle $BAC = 58^\circ$, angle $ABC = 47^\circ$, $AD = 9.4$ m and $CD = 11.8$ m.

Calculate the length of the fence $AC$. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Work inside triangle ABC first; it is the only triangle with two angles in it.
AB faces the unmarked vertex C, so find angle ACB before pairing anything.
AC faces the 47° at B.
parts.workedSolution: Angle $ACB = 180^\circ - 58^\circ - 47^\circ = 75^\circ$. Then $\dfrac{AC}{\sin 47^\circ} = \dfrac{12.6}{\sin 75^\circ}$, so $AC = \dfrac{12.6\sin 47^\circ}{\sin 75^\circ} = 9.5401\ldots = 9.54$ m (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: Triangle ACD has been entered too early: it has two sides but no angle yet, so nothing can be found there. Triangle ABC holds two angles and a side, which is where the question opens.

parts.stem: Calculate the size of angle $ADC$. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

scheme.examinerNote: 51.7 indicates a rounded AC was used: M1 MA1 only.

hints: Triangle ACD now has all three sides.
AC faces the angle at D, so AC² is the square that is subtracted.
Use the stored value of AC from part (a), not 9.54.
parts.workedSolution: In triangle $ACD$ all three sides are known. $\cos ADC = \dfrac{9.4^2 + 11.8^2 - 9.5401\ldots^2}{2 \times 9.4 \times 11.8} = 0.61569\ldots$, so angle $ADC = 51.9975\ldots = 52.0^\circ$ (1 d.p.).

commonErrors.feedback: Both method marks stand: this is the answer that comes from putting 9.5 back in instead of the stored value. Use the calculator's memory between parts and the answer lands on 52.0.

parts.stem: Calculate the area of triangle $ACD$. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Which two sides meet at D?
AD and CD meet at D, so the angle from part (b) is the included angle.
parts.workedSolution: $AD$ and $CD$ meet at $D$, so angle $ADC$ is the included angle. Area $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 9.4 \times 11.8 \times \sin(51.9975\ldots^\circ) = 43.7015\ldots = 43.7$ m$^2$ (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: That comes from using the 58° at A with AD and CD. Those two sides meet at D, so only angle ADC, the angle you found in part (b), belongs in the formula.

context.setting: Two triangular panels sharing an edge

figures.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 370 275' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='370' height='275' role='img' aria-label='Triangles PQR and QRS sharing QR, with angle PQR 52 degrees and angle RQS 71 degrees'><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'><path d='M34 90.7 L182 214.9'/><path d='M182 214.9 L336 167.8'/><path d='M336 167.8 L187.2 66.1'/><path d='M187.2 66.1 L34 90.7'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-linecap='round'><path d='M182 214.9 L187.2 66.1' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><path d='M159 195.6 A30 30 0 0 1 183.1 184.9'/><path d='M183.6 169 A46 46 0 0 1 226 201.5'/></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' font-size='13'><text x='96.4' y='170.6' text-anchor='middle'>9.6 cm</text><text x='166.6' y='143.9' text-anchor='middle'>7.4 cm</text><text x='162.9' y='176' text-anchor='middle'>52%C2%B0</text><text x='218.5' y='171.3' text-anchor='middle'>71%C2%B0</text><text x='19.6' y='91.5' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>P</text><text x='181.5' y='234.9' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>Q</text><text x='187.7' y='56.1' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>R</text><text x='350.7' y='176' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>S</text><text x='364' y='16' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>diagram not drawn</text><text x='364' y='29' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>accurately</text></g></svg>
figures.alt: Two triangles sharing the side QR: triangle PQR on the left with PQ 9.6 cm, QR 7.4 cm and angle PQR 52 degrees, and triangle QRS on the right with angle RQS 71 degrees. RS is to be found.

parts.stem:
Two triangular panels $PQR$ and $QRS$ share the edge $QR$ and have the same area.

$PQ = 9.6$ cm, $QR = 7.4$ cm, angle $PQR = 52^\circ$ and angle $RQS = 71^\circ$.

Find the length of $RS$.

Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

scheme.for: ½ × 9.6 × 7.4 × sin 52 = ½ × 7.4 × QS × sin 71 (oe; both areas written with the correct included angles)
QS = 9.6 sin 52 ÷ sin 71, or area PQR = 28.0 used with ½ × 7.4 × QS × sin 71 = 28.0

hints: Write down what each area is in terms of ½ab sin C; the shared side 7.4 cm appears in both.
Equal areas gives an equation with QS as the only unknown; the 7.4 cancels.
With QS found, triangle QRS has two sides and the angle between them.
parts.workedSolution: Area $PQR = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 9.6 \times 7.4 \times \sin 52^\circ$ and area $QRS = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 7.4 \times QS \times \sin 71^\circ$. Setting them equal and cancelling $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 7.4$ gives $QS = \dfrac{9.6\sin 52^\circ}{\sin 71^\circ} = 8.0007\ldots$ cm. Then in triangle $QRS$, $RS^2 = 7.4^2 + 8.0007\ldots^2 - 2 \times 7.4 \times 8.0007\ldots \times \cos 71^\circ = 80.2216\ldots$, so $RS = 8.9566\ldots = 8.96$ cm (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: The area of PQR is right and earns the first mark, but it is a stepping stone, not the answer. Put it equal to the area of QRS to get QS, then use the cosine rule for RS. Summer 2025 examiners saw many scripts that stopped at exactly this line.
QS is found and three marks are safe. The question asks for RS, which needs the cosine rule in triangle QRS with the 71° between QR and QS.

figures.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox='0 0 360 268' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' width='360' height='268' role='img' aria-label='Quadrilateral ABCD, area 60 square centimetres, with no diagonal drawn'><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.6' stroke-linecap='round' stroke-linejoin='round'><path d='M40 190.6 L127.5 61'/><path d='M127.5 61 L320 88.1'/><path d='M320 88.1 L251.3 207'/><path d='M251.3 207 L40 190.6'/></g><g fill='none' stroke='currentColor' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-linecap='round'><path d='M294.3 84.4 A26 26 0 0 0 307 110.6'/></g><g fill='currentColor' font-family='system-ui,sans-serif' font-size='13'><text x='68.8' y='119.7' text-anchor='middle'>7.4 cm</text><text x='226.3' y='60.7' text-anchor='middle'>9.2 cm</text><text x='301.3' y='160.5' text-anchor='middle'>6.5 cm</text><text x='281.4' y='110.9' text-anchor='middle'>68%C2%B0</text><text x='25.9' y='200.8' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>A</text><text x='118.5' y='54' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>B</text><text x='334.1' y='88' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>C</text><text x='261.6' y='222.9' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='600'>D</text><text x='12' y='252' text-anchor='start' font-size='12'>Area of ABCD = 60 cm%C2%B2</text><text x='354' y='16' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>diagram not drawn</text><text x='354' y='29' text-anchor='end' font-size='11'>accurately</text></g></svg>
figures.alt: Quadrilateral ABCD with no diagonal drawn. AB is 7.4 cm, BC is 9.2 cm, CD is 6.5 cm, angle BCD is 68 degrees and the whole quadrilateral has an area of 60 square centimetres.

parts.stem:
A logo is the quadrilateral $ABCD$.

$AB = 7.4$ cm, $BC = 9.2$ cm, $CD = 6.5$ cm and angle $BCD = 68^\circ$.

The area of the whole logo is $60$ cm$^2$.

Calculate the size of angle $ABD$.

Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: BD drawn or implied, and area BCD = ½ × 9.2 × 6.5 × sin 68 = 27.7 (accept 27.7 to 27.8)
½ × 7.4 × (their BD) × sin ABD = their area ABD

scheme.examinerNote: The diagram shows angle ABD is acute, so the acute value is the one expected; the ambiguous case is excluded from this specification.

hints: Nothing in the quadrilateral can be worked out as it stands. Is there one line you could add that would make a triangle you can finish?
Draw BD. Triangle BCD then has two sides and the angle between them, so its area and its third side BD are both available.
The area of triangle ABD is what is left of the 60 cm².
In triangle ABD you know two sides and the area, so run ½ab sin C backwards.
parts.workedSolution: Nothing can be done to the quadrilateral as it stands, so draw $BD$. Triangle $BCD$ then has two sides and the angle between them, so start there. Area $BCD = \tfrac{1}{2} \times 9.2 \times 6.5 \times \sin 68^\circ = 27.7227\ldots$ cm$^2$, so area $ABD = 60 - 27.7227\ldots = 32.2772\ldots$ cm$^2$. The cosine rule gives $BD^2 = 9.2^2 + 6.5^2 - 2 \times 9.2 \times 6.5 \times \cos 68^\circ = 82.0870\ldots$, so $BD = 9.0601\ldots$ cm. In triangle $ABD$, $AB$ and $BD$ meet at $B$, so $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 7.4 \times 9.0601\ldots \times \sin ABD = 32.2772\ldots$, giving $\sin ABD = 0.96284\ldots$ and angle $ABD = 74.3326\ldots = 74.3^\circ$ (1 d.p.).

commonErrors.feedback: No line has been added, so there is no triangle to work in yet. Draw BD: triangle BCD then has two sides and the angle between them, so its area and BD both come out, and the rest of the 60 cm² belongs to triangle ABD. Summer 2024 examiners reported that the extra line was exactly what separated the full-mark answers.
The chain is right and seven marks are safe. Rounded values of the area or of BD were carried forward; keeping the full display through all three stages brings the answer back to 74.3°.
That is 180° − 74.3°. The ambiguous case is excluded from this specification, and the diagram shows the angle at B is acute, so 74.3° is the value to give.

figures.alt: Airfield A with a north line. The flight goes from A on a bearing of 062 degrees for 48 km to B, where a second north line is drawn, then on a bearing of 155 degrees for 37 km to C. AC is drawn.

parts.stem:
A search aircraft leaves airfield $A$ and flies 48 km on a bearing of $062^\circ$ to point $B$. It then turns and flies 37 km on a bearing of $155^\circ$ to point $C$.

Show that angle $ABC = 87^\circ$.

scheme.for: bearing of A from B = 062 + 180 = 242 (or the co-interior angle 180 − 62 = 118 used at B)

scheme.examinerNote: A bare 87 with no working earns nothing on a Show that.

hints: Draw the north line at B and mark the direction back to A.
Both directions at B must be measured from the same north line before you subtract.
parts.workedSolution: The bearing of $A$ from $B$ is the back bearing $062^\circ + 180^\circ = 242^\circ$. The bearing of $C$ from $B$ is $155^\circ$, and both are measured clockwise from the north line at $B$, so angle $ABC = 242^\circ - 155^\circ = 87^\circ$ as required.

commonErrors.feedback: 155° − 62° = 93° uses two bearings measured at different points. At B, the direction back to A is 242°, and 242° − 155° = 87°. The two answers are supplementary, which is why a size check alone will not catch this.

parts.stem: Calculate the distance $AC$. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Two sides with the angle from part (a) between them.
AC faces the 87°, so AC² is on the left of the cosine rule.

commonErrors.feedback: Two marks are secure; the cosine rule produces AC², so the square root is the step that remains.

parts.stem: Calculate the bearing of $C$ from $A$. Give your answer to the nearest degree.

scheme.examinerNote: Accept 101 or 101°; a bearing given as 100 suggests the rounded AC was used.

hints: The sine rule now has a complete pair: 87° with AC facing it.
The angle you find is inside the triangle, at A.
A bearing is measured from the north line at A, so add the angle to 062°.
parts.workedSolution: $\dfrac{\sin BAC}{37} = \dfrac{\sin 87^\circ}{59.0516\ldots}$, so $\sin BAC = 0.62571\ldots$ and angle $BAC = 38.7343\ldots^\circ$. $AC$ lies clockwise of $AB$, so the bearing of $C$ from $A$ is $062^\circ + 38.7343\ldots^\circ = 100.7343\ldots^\circ = 101^\circ$ to the nearest degree.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the angle inside the triangle at A, and the two method marks stand. A bearing is measured clockwise from north at A, so it is 062° + 38.7° = 101°.

findTheMistake.stem: Órla was asked to calculate angle $ADC$ in a field $ABCD$. In triangle $ABC$, angle $BAC = 58^\circ$, angle $ABC = 47^\circ$ and $AB = 12.6$ m; in triangle $ACD$, $AD = 9.4$ m and $CD = 11.8$ m. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The method is right the whole way through. On line 3 the diagonal was rounded to 9.5 before it was used again; the display read 9.540128…, and that difference of four hundredths moves the final angle from 52.0° to 51.7°.
correction: AC = 12.6 sin 47 ÷ sin 75 = 9.540128… (keep the display, write 9.54 m only if the question asks for a length)
findTheMistake.feedback: Everything that was for method is safe: the angle sum, the sine rule, the rearranged cosine rule. Only the final accuracy mark goes, because the value fed forward was a rounded one. Keep the long value in the calculator between stages, and round once on the answer line. CCEA marks the most accurate figure seen anywhere in your working, so the full value costs nothing and protects the last mark.

findTheMistake.stem: A diagram shows triangles $PQR$ and $QRS$ meeting along $QR$. $PQ = 9.6$ cm, $QR = 7.4$ cm, angle $PQR = 52^\circ$ and angle $RQS = 71^\circ$. Dáire was asked for the area of triangle $PQR$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The two sides chosen are right, but 71° is the angle between QR and QS, not between PQ and QR. The angle that belongs in the formula is the one at the vertex where the two chosen sides meet, which is angle PQR = 52°.
findTheMistake.feedback: No method mark here, because the formula was not used with the angle it needs, and an accuracy mark cannot follow a method mark that was not earned. When a diagram carries two angles at the same vertex, ring the one that sits between your two sides before you write the formula. The answer 33.6 is close enough to be believable, which is what makes this slip worth drilling: it never looks like an error on the page.

findTheMistake.stem: A sail $KLM$ has $KL = 8.3$ m, $KM = 11.6$ m and angle $K = 74^\circ$. Caoimhe was asked to calculate $LM$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Pythagoras' theorem was used in a triangle that has no right angle. The 74° angle was given precisely because the triangle is not right-angled, and the cosine rule is the version of Pythagoras that handles any angle.
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing is awarded for this route, so it is worth a habit rather than a repair: before any trigonometry, look for the right-angle square on the diagram. If there is none, the tools are the sine rule, the cosine rule and ½ab sin C. Notice too that the answer 14.3 m is longer than the correct 12.3 m — dropping the −2bc cos A term always overstates the side when the angle is acute. Summer 2025 examiners reported many different incorrect approaches on a single sine-rule question; choosing the tool deliberately is what separates them.

prompts.prompt: State the sine rule, and say what the triangle must give you before you can use it.
prompts.answer: $\dfrac{a}{\sin A} = \dfrac{b}{\sin B} = \dfrac{c}{\sin C}$. You need one complete pair — a side with the angle opposite it — plus one more piece: another angle (to find a side) or another side (to find an angle).

prompts.prompt: State the cosine rule, and its rearrangement for an angle.
prompts.answer: $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$, and $\cos A = \dfrac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$. The first form is on the formula sheet; the rearranged form is not, so it has to be known.

prompts.prompt: Give the area formula for any triangle, and say exactly which angle it uses.
prompts.answer: Area $= \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$, where $C$ is the angle between the two sides $a$ and $b$ — the angle at the vertex where those two sides meet, never any other angle in the triangle.

prompts.prompt: How do you decide between the sine rule and the cosine rule?
prompts.answer: Label the triangle, then look at what is given. Two angles and any side, or a side with the angle opposite it: sine rule. Two sides with the angle between them, or all three sides: cosine rule. If neither fits, that triangle is not where the question starts: find another one in the diagram, or draw the line that creates one.

prompts.prompt: In triangle $ABC$, which side is $a$, and why does it matter?
prompts.answer: $a$ is $BC$, the side opposite angle $A$ — the side that does not touch $A$. It matters because both rules are written in those letters: the side you subtract in the cosine rule, and the side you pair in the sine rule, are always the ones facing the angle involved.

prompts.prompt: A route runs from $A$ to $B$ on a bearing of $070^\circ$, then from $B$ to $C$ on a bearing of $145^\circ$. How do you get the angle $ABC$?
prompts.answer: Take the back bearing first: the bearing of $A$ from $B$ is $070^\circ + 180^\circ = 250^\circ$. Both directions are now measured from the north line at $B$, so angle $ABC = 250^\circ - 145^\circ = 105^\circ$. Mark it on the diagram before choosing a rule.

prompts.prompt: You find a diagonal of $7.483921\ldots$ cm and need it in the next stage. What do you write, and what do you use?
prompts.answer: Write the full value (or 7.48 cm on an answer line that asks for 3 significant figures), but use the stored display in the next calculation. Rounding part-way moves the final answer and loses the accuracy mark; CCEA marks the most accurate figure seen in your working.

prompts.prompt: A diagram marks two angles at the same vertex, $52^\circ$ and $71^\circ$, and you want the area of the triangle whose two sides meet there. Which do you use?
prompts.answer: The one that lies between your two sides. Ring the two sides on the diagram first, then take the angle in the fork they make. Using the other angle gives an answer of a believable size, so nothing on the page warns you.

prompts.prompt: Two things often slip when the cosine rule is typed into a calculator. What are they?
prompts.answer: First, $2bc\cos A$ must be multiplied out before it is subtracted, not $b^2 + c^2 - 2bc$ then multiplied by $\cos A$. Second, the rule gives $a^2$, so the square root is still to come. A quick size check catches both: the third side lies between the difference and the sum of the other two.

prompts.prompt: Which of these three formulae are printed on the Higher formula sheet, and what is not?
prompts.answer: All three are printed on page 2: the sine rule, the cosine rule in the form $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A$, and Area $= \frac{1}{2}ab\sin C$. What is not printed is the rearrangement $\cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2) \div 2bc$, the labelling convention, and the decision about which rule to use — and those are where the marks actually are.

prompts.prompt: Your calculator gives $\sin^{-1}(0.9628\ldots) = 74.3^\circ$. Should you also offer $105.7^\circ$?
prompts.answer: No. The ambiguous case of the sine rule is excluded by the CCEA Teacher Guidance, so a question will not be set where two answers are wanted. Give the value your calculator returns, and check it against the diagram.

prompts.prompt: A quadrilateral has an area you are given, three sides and one angle. The final answer wanted is an angle. What is your plan?
prompts.answer: Draw the diagonal that splits it into two triangles. In the triangle with two sides and the angle between them, find its area and the diagonal (½ab sin C, then the cosine rule). Subtract that area from the total to get the other triangle's area, then run ½ab sin C backwards in that triangle to get $\sin$ of the angle, and finish with $\sin^{-1}$.

findings.asked: A multi-step trigonometry problem in non-right-angled triangles.
findings.wentWrong: Nearly 40% solved it; over 40% could not find a first step; the rest made a sensible start in trigonometry but could not carry it through.
findings.rule: Decide which triangle has enough information to start, and say why.

findings.asked: Closing question needing the cosine rule, sine rule and the area formula after adding one line to the diagram.
findings.wentWrong: About a sixth got full marks; many attempted it. The unlock was drawing one extra line.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Added the line that created a triangle with three known pieces, then moved through cosine rule, sine rule and half ab sin C in order.
findings.rule: If no triangle is solvable, draw a line that makes one.

findings.asked: A testing trigonometry question with a specific correct starting point.
findings.wentWrong: Weaker candidates did not see that the cosine rule had to come first.
findings.rule: Three sides, or two sides and the included angle: cosine rule first.

findings.asked: A single non-right-angled triangle, three marks, one rule needed.
findings.wentWrong: Many answers were completely correct, and many others took approaches that could not work at all.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the rule down, substituted into it, and rearranged once.
findings.rule: Choose the tool from what the triangle gives you, and write the rule before the numbers.

findings.asked: Equal areas to find a side, then the cosine rule, for six marks.
findings.wentWrong: Nearly a third finished; weaker candidates could not find a logical start; many wrote the equal-area equation and stopped.
findings.rule: Area = half ab sin C can be solved for a side, then feed it into the cosine rule.

findings.asked: Bearings combined with the sine rule.
findings.wentWrong: About a quarter got full marks; converting bearings into the triangle's angles was the hurdle.
findings.rule: Mark every angle from the bearings on the diagram before choosing a rule.

findings.asked: Areas and the cosine rule in an eight-mark final problem.
findings.wentWrong: Most scored some marks; about a quarter got all eight.
